"Mummy, why did everyone stand up when Mama came in?"
"He's a senior officer, Pradeep. People respect his post."
"But when Papa came in, nobody stood up. Bua didn't even give him a chair."
Indu was quiet. "Papa drives a bus. Some people think that's a small job."
"Is it small?"
"What do you think? Who takes a hundred people to work every morning?"
"...Papa."
"And who brought Dadi to the hospital at midnight, in the rain?"
"Papa."
"Then is his job small?"
Pradeep shook his head. "But why do they treat him like that?"
"Because some grown-ups forget that honest work is honest work. Don't you forget it."
Pradeep walked over, pulled out a chair, and put it beside his father.

qa.a: Papa brought Dadi to the hospital at midnight, in the rain.

qa.a: Pradeep felt confused and a little hurt, noticing that relatives treated his father as less important.

grounding: A child notices relatives treat a senior officer better than his bus-driver father, and his mother teaches that honest work carries dignity.

I'm twelve now. I still remember that clapping. And Zeenat's words.

Class teacher's note, Class 4, "My Parent's Job" day.
Children spoke about their parents' work. When Sudha said her mother was a doctor, the class said "Wow!" When Keerthana stood up, she said quietly, "My appa is only a driver," and sat down fast.
I asked her, "Only?" She shrugged. "My aunty says drivers aren't important."
I asked who had come to school by car, bus or van. Almost every hand went up. "Who drove?" Silence, then giggles, then understanding. Sudha said, "My mummy couldn't reach the hospital without a driver."
Keerthana looked up.
I told them that every honest job has dignity, and that "only" is not a word for anyone's work.
Next step: I've asked Keerthana's father to come and talk to the class about his day.

In Accra, Chidi, twenty-five, had been a junior engineer at the construction firm for a year. He'd learned to stay quiet in meetings; the old director hated being questioned.
The new director, Mr. Kofi Mensah, started differently. At his first review, he put his design on the screen and said, "Please, find the problems. I'd rather hear them now than on site."
A young woman from the drawing team said, carefully, "Sir, the beam spacing on level three may be too wide." Everyone froze.
Mr. Mensah studied it. "You're right. Thank you, Abena. That could have cost us." He shook her hand in front of everyone.
Chidi felt something loosen in his chest. At the next meeting, he pointed out a drainage issue. Kofi thanked him too.
Years later, Chidi still told junior engineers about that director.

Pooja, you're upset that your father pays you "pocket money" instead of a salary at the shop? Let your Sangeeta Bua tell you something.
When I was twenty-four, I worked in my father's sari shop in Varanasi. Six days a week, ten hours a day. I did the accounts, handled the customers, even the suppliers. My brother came in once a week and was called "the owner's son." I was called "helping out."
I got no salary. When I asked, Papa said, "It's all family money anyway." I felt invisible, and I was ashamed to feel that way.
One day I wrote everything down: what I did, how many hours, what a hired accountant would earn. I sat with Papa and my brother and asked for a title, a fixed salary and a written role. Papa was hurt. But he agreed.
So, Pooja: write it down, and talk.

It was the week before Diwali, and the printing press in Lucknow was drowning in orders for greeting cards. Yamini, twenty-five, had been working there under her uncle for three years. She handled clients, designs and deadlines. She had no fixed salary, only "whatever you need, just ask."
At ten p.m., her uncle shouted at her in front of the workers for a delayed order. Her cousin Shreya, who came in twice a week, was praised for bringing tea.
Yamini went to the storeroom and sat on the paper bundles, shaking. It wasn't the shouting. It was that she had no name for what she was.

Vasudha, twenty-four, had run the counter at her father's sweet shop in Nagpur since she finished college. She knew every supplier, every regular customer, every festival order. But when her father introduced her, he said, "My daughter helps sometimes."
She earned nothing fixed. When she needed money for a course, she had to ask him like a child.

Class teacher's note, Class 11, essay review.
Raghav, 16, wrote an essay titled "The Day My Father Paid." He described watching his father hand money to a clerk at the property registration office to speed up their papers. He wrote, "Papa said everyone does it. I don't know if I'm angry or impressed. Maybe both."
In class discussion, Elizabeth argued that paying is sometimes the only way to get anything done. Raghav said, quietly, "But then it never stops."
I did not judge his father in front of the class. I asked the students to discuss why shortcuts feel normal, who loses when people pay, and what honest options exist, such as public grievance systems and online applications.
Raghav stayed after class and said he felt confused and a little ashamed. I told him that noticing it at all was the start of choosing differently.
Next step: a class session on citizens' rights and complaint channels.

qa.a: It was titled "The Day My Father Paid."

qa.a: Raghav felt confused and a little ashamed, unsure whether he was angry or impressed.
